# All-length half-integer triangle chains: the high positive-normal sector

This theorem controls a full sector of the actual oblique halfspaces at
the central own centroid. It does not establish the remaining positive
normal sector or OC for arbitrary mixed-integer sources.

## Theorem

Let T=conv(0,e_1,e_2), V=area(T)=1/2. For h=0,...,m let the original
integer fibers at bases -h and h+1 be r_h T, where

    r_0=R>0, R>=r_1>=...>=r_m>=0,
    r_(h-1)-r_h <= r_h-r_(h+1)  (1<=h<m).

Put t=R/3. For every a in [2/3,1] and every beta>=0, the actual cap

    H={-beta z+a x_1+(1-a)x_2>=t}

satisfies

    H_2(S intersect H)>=(2/9)H_2(S),                        (1)

where S is this finite union of the original simplex fibers. Its
center y=(0,t,t) is one deterministic point of S. The same conclusion
holds for the opposite sign of the integer tilt, by the proved
cross-label monotonicity comparison for paired fibers. Positive-area
mass on any ambient cap boundary is handled by the exact closed-cap
formula; for these nonzero continuous normals every fiber boundary
has area zero. Terminal zero radii also have zero H_2 measure.

The proof below uses no fixed bound on m and no asymptotic replacement
of its fiber sums. Common invertible affine maps in the continuous
coordinates can be tracked by their constant area determinant as in
the earlier restricted theorem.

## Step 1: the deficit-monotone affine reduction

Let F_r(u) be the normalized triangle tail at continuous normal
(a,1-a), and put gamma=4/9. The exact cap deficit is

    D(r)=sum_(h=0)^m [F_(r_h)(t-beta h)
                        +F_(r_h)(t+beta(h+1))-gamma r_h^2].

The theorem in `candidate a15fce1d462289cc`
proves that for this fixed cap there is an affine radius profile

    l_h=R-lambda h,  0<=lambda<=R/m,

whose EACH paired deficit is at most the corresponding original one.
That theorem includes its full elementary proof: the paired deficit's
unique minimizing radius is

    rho_h=min{(t-beta h)_+/d_a,(2t+beta)/(a+d_a)},
    d_a=(a+4)/9;

the radius-drop slopes (R-r_h)/h are nondecreasing while
(R-rho_h)/h are decreasing. A separating slope puts l_h between the
original radius and its exact scalar minimizer at each index. This
proves deficit monotonicity directly, including completely empty caps.

Consequently it suffices to prove (1) for affine profiles. If m=0,
the own central fiber alone pays gamma R^2, exactly the target for
two equal fibers, by the ordinary triangle centroid inequality.

## Step 2: a pairwise closure and extension to the maximal affine leg

For an affine profile, if beta>=lambda/3, then at every original left
fiber

    t-beta h <=(R-lambda h)/3=l_h/3.

The cap therefore contains a halfspace through that fiber's own
centroid, and its left member alone pays at least gamma l_h^2.
Summing proves the target. This includes lambda=0.

It remains to consider lambda>0 and 0<=beta<lambda/3. Scale all radii,
thresholds, and integer-tilt coefficients by R, which multiplies all
areas by the same R^2. Thus assume R=1, put k=lambda/R, and note
0<k<=1 when m>=1. Write the dimensionless beta again as beta. Both
normalized thresholds along the continuous affine leg have positive
derivative:

    d/dh [(1/3-beta h)/(1-kh)]
       =(k/3-beta)/(1-kh)^2>0,
    d/dh [(1/3+beta(h+1))/(1-kh)]
       =[beta+k(1/3+beta)]/(1-kh)^2>0.                     (2)

By homogeneity F_r(u)=r^2 F_1(u/r), the paired deficit divided by r^2
is consequently nonincreasing with h while r=1-kh>0. If the original
affine chain were violating, some positive-radius paired deficit
would be negative. Every later positive-radius paired deficit would
then be nonpositive. Extend the same affine line through every index
with 1-kh>0, adding a possible final zero radius without effect. All
new paired deficits are nonpositive, so the extended chain would
still violate. It is thus enough to prove nonnegativity of the
deficit of this maximal finite affine leg.

This extension is an exact construction at original integer bases;
it is not an integral approximation. If the original chain already
ends at a zero radius, it is already maximal. Negative radii are
never included.

## Step 3: two exact arithmetic quadratic sums

For p>=0 and l>0 define the finite sum, written conveniently as

    S(p,l)=sum_(h=0)^infinity (p-lh)_+^2.                  (3)

Only finitely many terms are nonzero. Put

    b=1/(3a), P=1-b, z=beta/(a k), A=1/(2-3b).

The ranges are

    1/3<=b<=1/2,  0<=z<b,  0<k<=1.                      (4)

Since beta<k/3, the left threshold at every positive-radius original
fiber is at least r/3, and the right threshold is larger. Since
a>=2/3, both thresholds lie in the upper proper triangle-tail branch
or beyond its supporting vertex. Therefore

    F_r(u)=A(r-u/a)_+^2.

The maximal affine cap area divided by V is EXACTLY

    A[S(P,k(1-z))+S(P-kz,k(1+z))],                        (5)

and its total normalized source area is 2S(1,k). To check that (5)
does not add fictitious positive mass beyond the affine leg, evaluate
its first affine expression at h=1/k: its value is z-b<0. Its slope
is negative. The second expression is also negative there and has
negative slope. Thus both infinite sums vanish beyond the last
nonnegative original radius.

The desired assertion is consequently the concrete arithmetic
inequality

    A[S(P,k(1-z))+S(P-kz,k(1+z))] >=(4/9)S(1,k).          (6)

## Lemma 1: elementary upper and lower bounds for (3)

For p>=0 and l>0,

    S(p,l)>=p^2,
    S(p,l)>=p^3/(3l)+p^2/2.                              (7)

For 0<k<=1,

    S(1,k)<=1/(3k)+1/2+k/5.                              (8)

Proof. The first bound in (7) is its first summand. The function
(p-lx)_+^2 is convex on [0,infinity); on every unit interval its
integral is at most the trapezoid average of its endpoint values.
Summing the finite nonzero trapezoids gives
integral_0^infinity (p-lx)_+^2 dx<=S(p,l)-p^2/2, proving (7).

For (8), put N=floor(1/k) and delta=1/k-N in [0,1). Elementary sums
of 1,j,j^2, or direct expansion of k^2 sum_(j=0)^N(j+delta)^2, give

    S(1,k)=1/(3k)+1/2+k/6-(k^2/3)B_3(delta),
    B_3(delta)=delta(delta-1/2)(delta-1).

For delta<=1/2 this cubic is nonnegative. For delta>=1/2,

    -B_3(delta)=delta(delta-1/2)(1-delta)<=1/16,

because delta<=1 and the two nonnegative factors delta-1/2 and
1-delta have sum 1/2 and product at most 1/16. Therefore

    S(1,k)<=1/(3k)+1/2+k/6+k^2/48
           <=1/(3k)+1/2+3k/16
           <=1/(3k)+1/2+k/5.

All of these are exact finite-sum bounds, including integral phase
1/k and all truncation knots.

## Lemma 2: the explicit scalar certificate

On the CLOSED box 1/3<=b<=1/2, 0<=z<=b, 0<k<=1, put

    f_k(p,l)=(1-k)[p^3/(3l)+p^2/2]+k p^2.

Then

    [f_k(1-b,k(1-z))+f_k(1-b-kz,k(1+z))]/(2-3b)
       >(4/9)[1/(3k)+1/2+k/5].                            (9)

Here all p values are nonnegative, all l values are positive, and
the factor 2-3b is positive.

Proof. Let H be the left side minus the right side of (9). Multiplying
by the explicitly positive denominator

    D=270k(2-3b)(1-z^2)

gives the polynomial N(b,z,k) printed below. Substitute z=bv, with
0<=v<=1. Map b=1/3+x/6 and v=y. On each of the two k intervals
[0,1/2] and [1/2,1], map k=k_0+w/2, where k_0 is respectively
0 and 1/2. The resulting polynomial has degree at most four in each
of x,y,w. Expand it in the tensor Bernstein basis

    sum_(i,j,l=0)^4 c_(i,j,l) B_i^4(x) B_j^4(y) B_l^4(w),
    B_i^4(x)=binom(4,i)x^i(1-x)^(4-i).

All 125 coefficients on each box are strictly positive. Their exact
minimum is 5/2 on the first box and 331/384 on the second. A complete
exact list and independent reconstruction formula are in the
certificate JSON and verifier specified below. Since this basis is
nonnegative and sums to one, the claimed strict polynomial positivity
follows on both boxes, including their boundaries. For k>0 division
by D proves (9). The endpoint k=0 is used only for the polynomial
certificate and never as a denominator.

The numerator is

    180b^3k-180b^3
    -540b^2k^2z^2+270b^2k^2z+270b^2k^2
    -270b^2kz-270b^2k+540b^2
    -540bk^3z^3+270bk^3z^2+270bk^3z
    +738bk^2z^2-270bk^2z-468bk^2
    -180bkz^2+540bkz+180bk-120bz^2-420b
    -225k^4z^4+90k^4z^3+135k^4z^2
    -45k^3z^4+450k^3z^3-135k^3z^2-270k^3z
    -222k^2z^2+222k^2+120kz^2-270kz-30k+80z^2+100.

For explicit reconstruction, if a mapped power expansion is
sum a_(p,q,r)x^p y^q w^r, its Bernstein coefficient is the finite
rational sum

    c_(i,j,l)=sum_(p<=i,q<=j,r<=l) a_(p,q,r)
       binom(i,p)binom(j,q)binom(l,r)
       /[binom(4,p)binom(4,q)binom(4,r)].

Thus this lemma is certified by elementary polynomial identities and
rational inequalities, not by numerical optimization or finite
parameter sampling.

## Completion of the theorem

By (7), S(p,l) is at least any convex combination of the two displayed
lower bounds; in particular S(p,l)>=f_k(p,l) because 0<=k<=1.
Apply (9) to the two exact sums in (5), then apply (8). This proves
(6), with strict surplus in the remaining beta<lambda/3 regime.
The pairwise case handles beta>=lambda/3. Step 2 rules out every
violating finite affine prefix, and Step 1 rules out every violating
original concave radius chain. This proves (1) for arbitrary m.

## Certificate artifacts and proof scope

The generation script is
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/certify_half_integer_affine_high_sector_candidate.py`; despite its
historical filename, the displayed two-box polynomial certificates
are exact. It verifies the rational identity H=N/D and reconstructs
all 250 Bernstein coefficients using rational arithmetic. The full
coefficient artifact is `../assets/pk-nov6/computations/half-integer-affine-high-sector-bernstein.json`.

The affine reduction independently passed 86,820 exact rational
minimizer and pointwise-deficit checks in
`../assets/pk-nov6/computations/verify_half_integer_affine_radius_reduction.py`; those checks are
supplementary to its complete proof. The earlier mass-localized
m<=11 reduction is no longer needed for this high-sector theorem.
The lower sector 1/2<=a<2/3 remains outside the theorem, and neither
arbitrary nonsymmetric sources nor general dimensions are settled.
